column4: Joseph's brothers ask that he be sent with them to roam or graze and play; this pastoral departure immediately precedes the child's separation from his father and frames him as the vulnerable member taken out with the company.
Jacob fears that a wolf will eat Joseph while the brothers are heedless of him; the owner-parent anticipates exactly the loss of one entrusted member while its keepers fail to watch.

The brothers return claiming that a wolf ate Joseph while they raced; their story presents the missing member as an animal-like pastoral loss, while the surrounding narrative preserves the father's knowledge that the account is false.
A brother proposes putting Joseph in the well so that a passing caravan will pick him up; it deliberately turns a known child into an apparently ownerless foundling awaiting a finder.
The Egyptian who acquires the found Joseph orders that his lodging be made honorable; the lost child of 12:19 moves into shelter, though separated from the father who knows him.
Joseph calls the human master who housed him “my rabb” and says that master made his lodging good; the ayah directly joins the section's owner-sense of Rabb to a protected dwelling.
The infant Moses is cast into the river, taken by an enemy, and kept under God's watch and bestowed love; apparent abandonment is bounded by an Owner who never loses sight of the exposed child.
Moses' sister tracks him, he is returned to his mother, rescued, tested, and brought at a measured time; this completes the lost child's recovery into maternal shelter and care.
Moses' mother is told to cast him into the river without fear because God will return him to her; separation from the mother begins under an explicit promise of recovery.
Pharaoh's household picks the infant from the water; like the section's found stray, the vulnerable being is taken in by people other than the one who knows he is missing.
Moses' mother tells his sister to follow him, and she watches from a distance unnoticed; the separated one's true family actively tracks rather than forgets him.
After other nursing women are withheld from Moses, his sister directs the finders toward a household that will care for him; the maternal bond becomes the path back to the proper shelter.
God returns Moses to his mother so that her eye may be comforted and she may know the promise is true; this is a complete Quranic recovery of one separated from the maternal side.
The emigrants and those who gave them shelter and support become protecting allies; the shelter-root describes incorporation of exposed people into a responsible community.
Those who believe, migrate, and shelter and support others are called the true believers; giving refuge is treated as the act that makes a scattered group one loyal company.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are created for riding and adornment; this supplies the Quranic setting for the section's secondary horse, rider, neck, and leading-animal details.

The ayah names the male and female of sheep and goats and asks whether either sex or what the female wombs contain was forbidden; with 6:144 it directly develops animal sex, maternity, and invented distinctions.
The messenger identifies the animal as “God's she-camel” and protects her allotted drink; female camel, named Owner, and ordered access to water meet in one warning.
As Solomon's ordered host reaches the ants, an ant calls its company into their dwellings so they will not be crushed; a voice gathers vulnerable creatures into shelter before a leading procession.
God has dispersed living creatures through the heavens and earth and is able to gather them whenever He wills; dispersal and recovered collection are explicitly held by one Owner.
God gathers all people and leaves none behind; the final collection answers the image of a procession with a laggard or missing member by explicitly excluding any omission.
God has fully encompassed and exactly counted every creature who comes to Him; the Owner knows each member individually, so no one in the gathered company is anonymous or lost.
God knows what the earth diminishes of human bodies and keeps a preserving record; this directly answers the claim of being “lost in the earth” with knowledge that retains every part.
The deniers ask whether, once “lost in the earth,” they can be newly created; the different bodily sense of ضَلَلْنَا extends the lost-animal image to dissolution and return to the Lord.
People emerge from graves like scattered locusts with humbled eyes; the animal comparison makes a dispersed multitude visible just before all hasten toward one caller.
On that day everyone follows the caller without deviation; the section's voice that recalls an animal becomes a universal summons whose company cannot stray from the call.
Believing men and women move with their light running before them toward the announced gardens; a guided forward company is visible immediately before the laggards of 57:13 are separated.
Hypocrites call to the believers to wait so they can take light, but are told to go back and a barrier divides them; the lagging members fail to rejoin the forward company.

The person of restricted provision must spend from what God gave, and God promises ease after hardship; constrained means, divine provision, and good arriving after delay closely extend the section's needy figure.
The poor are promised that God will enrich them from His bounty; this repeats the section's movement from need to sufficiency as a divine act.
The people are commanded to worship the Lord of “this House”; Rabb is identified through a fixed home, preparing the feeding and security named in 106:4.
The Lord of the House feeds against hunger and secures against fear; Owner, dwelling, provision, and safety combine as the human counterpart of a tended fold.
Within the cave-refuge passage, the one God guides is guided, while the one He lets stray has no protecting guide; shelter and direction are shown to depend on the same divine keeper.
A thirsty person follows a mirage in a level waste, finds nothing there, and instead finds God; the directionless desert search reaches the true Owner rather than the expected provision.
The foremost first emigrants and helpers are followed by later believers in excellence; the Quran explicitly makes a morally ordered company from leaders at the front and those following them.
Sun, moon, night, and day move in an order in which one does not overtake the other and each travels its course; this is a cosmic counterpart to the section's sequence of front and rear positions.
Birds above spread and fold their wings, and none holds them except the Merciful; the flying company remains upheld by its divine keeper rather than being abandoned.

Pharaoh leads his people on the Resurrection and brings them into the Fire, which the ayah calls an evil watering place; a leader drives his herd-like following to destructive water rather than safe pasture.
Disbelievers are driven in groups to Hell until its gates open; the group reaches a gated destination, but the fold has become punitive confinement.
Those mindful of their Lord are led in groups to the Garden until its gates open and its keepers greet them; paired with 39:71, this is the safe counterpart of a company brought home.
Pharaoh and his chiefs are made leaders who call toward the Fire; the foremost figures exercise precisely the opposite office from guides who bring those behind to safety.

Joseph's brothers accuse their father of manifest error because he loves Joseph and his brother more; within the lost-child story, ضَلَال denotes mistaken judgment rather than physical disappearance, preserving a secondary sense that matters.
When Jacob detects Joseph's scent, his family calls it his “old error”; the word for straying is applied to the very father whose recognition of the lost one is about to be vindicated.
One of the women returns to Moses and says her father calls him to repay the watering; the aid given to a delayed flock is answered by provision and entry into a household.
Lot wishes for strength or a firm support to which he could take refuge; the shelter-root names the need for a protecting place when one's household is exposed.
The hypocrites would bolt toward any refuge, cave, or place of entry they could find; their frantic search for shelter reverses the responsive return to a known keeper's fold.
Birds are made serviceable in the open sky and none holds them except God; the image gives the scattered flying creatures a keeper even away from any visible enclosure.
God makes homes places of rest and tents from livestock hides that are light during travel and encampment; the herd itself supplies a portable fold-like shelter.
Among livestock God creates animals for burden and others close to the ground, then commands people to eat His provision; the herd contains different positions and capacities under one Provider.
The she-camel has an assigned drinking day and the people have theirs; the animal's place in a measured watering order extends the section's ordered herd.
God sends the she-camel as a test and commands watchful patience; the keeper must recognize and protect a particular animal within the community.
Water is divided between the people and the she-camel, with each turn attended; the herd image gains an exact sequence of allotted access rather than a disorderly rush.
The opening oath depicts running horses breathing hard; it activates the section's equine leading and movement details, though here the animals charge rather than graze.
The horses raid at dawn; their forceful morning advance is a martial reversal of the section's herd quietly beginning to pasture early in the day.
The martyrs rejoice over those behind them who have not yet joined them; the ayah turns the rear of a company into members still expected to catch up.
Each community has a direction, people are told to race toward good, and God will bring everyone together; orientation, forward movement, and gathering share one ayah.
After hearing the ant's sheltering call, Solomon asks to be enabled to thank God for His blessing; the procession and gathered animals lead directly into remembrance of niʿma.
Birds with wings outspread each know their prayer and glorification, while God knows what they do; the flying ranks remain individually known to their Lord.
Everyone in the heavens and earth comes to the Merciful as a servant; it states the ownership relation that 19:94 then renders as exact encompassing and counting.
Each creature comes to God individually on the Resurrection; even within the universal gathering, every member reaches the Owner as a known individual.
Nothing as small as an atom in heaven or earth escapes God's knowledge, and all is in a clear record; it reinforces the boundary against any creature being truly unaccounted for.
The Prophet is told to turn away until the caller summons people to a terrible event; it supplies the voice whose gathered, animal-like respondents appear in 54:7.
The emerging multitude hastens toward the caller; it completes 54:7's scattered-locust image as a company converging on a voice.
The God-conscious are gathered to the Merciful as an honored delegation; this is a collective return to the Owner rather than an accidental massing.
The guilty are driven toward Hell as a thirsty herd; the pastoral verb and thirst make this the punitive opposite of livestock led to water and shelter.
At a single divine call, people emerge from the earth; the call recalls a dispersed creation into responsive presence.
God guides people through the darknesses of land and sea and sends winds before mercy; this directly answers the wilderness searcher who does not know which direction to take.
Stars are appointed so people may find their way through the darknesses of land and sea; the lost searcher is given concrete directional signs.
Landmarks and stars are means by which people are guided; the foremost guide of the section is complemented by fixed signs that orient a moving company.
Moses says the Lord gave every created thing its form and then guided it; guidance belongs to the creator-owner and extends beyond verbal instruction to each creature's fitted way.
God measures and then guides; the concise sequence presents direction as part of the ordering allotted to creatures rather than recovery by chance.
Praise belongs to God in the first life and the Hereafter; it is another formulation that places both ends of the section's line under one Lord.
The foremost are named twice as the foremost; this isolates the leading position whose closeness and destination are given in the following ayah.
The foremost of 56:10 are brought near to God; the head of the company is defined by proximity to its destination and Owner.
Inheritors of the Book divide into one who wrongs himself, one moderate, and one foremost in good; the single community forms a moral sequence with a leading rank.
Those who hasten in good deeds are described as foremost in them; the forward position becomes eagerness in delivering the very good that otherwise arrives late.
The same prophetic addressee is promised that ease accompanies hardship; this gives the section's delayed beneficence a closely related reassurance.
The promise of ease with hardship is repeated for emphasis; repetition makes eventual relief dependable for the addressee who was found exposed and needy.
Those unable to marry must remain chaste until God enriches them from His bounty; unlike 24:32's immediate promise, this ayah explicitly joins present lack to awaited sufficiency.
God produces humanity from one soul and knows its settled place and repository; the vocabulary of fixed and temporary location parallels the herd's stable place and its movement away from it.

After the straying-sheep judgment, God gives Solomon the right understanding and subjects birds to praise with David; it resolves the flock's disputed trespass and joins that scene to divinely ordered birds.
David judges that the owner of many ewes wronged the owner of one by demanding it, then repents; it supplies the moral boundary around the contested incorporation described in 38:23.
After Moses and his servant retrace the route of the lost fish, they find the servant of God they were meant to meet; recovering the missed place leads to the intended guide.
Horses and livestock are listed among the attractions of the nearer life, while the best return is with God; animal wealth is bounded by the first/latter valuation developed in the section.
Every blessing people possess is from God, and in distress they cry to Him; it makes the niʿma associated with the herd traceable to the same divine Owner.
